title: Symmetry-initialized Quantum Gibbs Sampling: A non-Abelian Asymmetry Cascade
authors: Soo-Jong Rey
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a quantum Gibbs sampler whose mixing bottleneck is a weakly broken symmetry, I show that the correct initialization is determined by representation theory. I first prove a general speedup-versus-prefactor dichotomy: by exactly eliminating slow-mode overlap, I convert a nominal prefactor reduction into a fundamental, asymptotic acceleration of the system's mixing time. I then show that when the bottleneck is a weakly broken symmetry, the otherwise exponentially expensive bottleneck eigenvector is the symmetry charge.For a non-Abelian group [MATH], I prove that the correct initialization target is the group-averaging asymmetry. Projecting this asymmetry out requires a [MATH]-invariant input. Partial, subgroup-invariant inputs produce a cascade of mixing-time speedups indexed by the subgroup lattice. Conversely, matching first moments alone is provably insufficient.The asymmetry is a directly measurable initialization target. I verify these results analytically and numerically in an [MATH] Davies sampler where total-spin multiplets constitute the slow modes. The predicted speedup cascade emerges with relaxation rates scaling linearly with the symmetry-breaking parameter. Finally, the model maps the boundaries of the asymmetry target, illustrating where the separate matching of conserved logical data becomes necessary.
tldr: This paper proves a speedup-versus-prefactor dichotomy for quantum Gibbs samplers with weakly broken symmetries, showing that symmetry-adapted initialization yields asymptotic mixing-time acceleration, and demonstrates a cascade of speedups for non-Abelian groups.
motivation: Quantum Gibbs sampling is crucial for quantum simulation and optimization, but mixing bottlenecks from weakly broken symmetries can be exponentially slow. The paper aims to find the correct initialization to overcome these bottlenecks.
method: The author uses representation theory to identify the bottleneck eigenvector as the symmetry charge, and proves that projecting out the group-averaging asymmetry (for non-Abelian groups) requires a group-invariant input. They analyze partial subgroup-invariant inputs and verify results analytically and numerically in an SU(2) Davies sampler.
result: The paper establishes a fundamental asymptotic speedup in mixing time when slow-mode overlap is eliminated, and shows that relaxation rates scale linearly with the symmetry-breaking parameter, with a cascade of speedups indexed by the subgroup lattice.
conclusion: The findings provide a practical initialization strategy for quantum Gibbs samplers, with the asymmetry as a measurable target, and highlight the necessity of matching conserved logical data beyond first moments.

title: Exact Minimum Measurement Dependence For Faithful Local Deterministic Models Of Multipartite GHZ-Mermin Correlations
authors: Aaron Alai
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bell derivations rest on locality, determinism, and measurement independence. Hall [Phys. Rev. Lett. 105, 250404 (2010)] priced the third assumption exactly for the singlet state, and in the Kochen-Specker analysis of Phys. Rev. A 84, 022102 (2011) priced the four tripartite Mermin perfect correlators at a surrendered fraction of 1/3, leaving open the problem of an optimal model for the Mermin state itself. This paper solves the faithful version of that problem -- every full correlator reproduced and every proper-subset marginal vanishing -- and extends it to thirteen parties. A reduction theorem shows the faithfulness constraints are free, so Hall's correlator-only threshold is promoted to the faithful value, F(3) = 1/3; linear-programming optima, certified exactly by an integer-arithmetic squeeze between a proven lower bound and an explicit construction, then give F(5) = 2/5, F(7) = 4/9, F(9) = 8/17, F(11) = 16/33, and F(13) = 32/65, each value through n = 11 repeated at the following even size. All computed points obey the closed law F = R/[2(R+1)] with R = 2^floor((n-1)/2) the Mermin violation ratio, a proven combinatorial lower bound is tight on every computed core, and a universal ceiling F <= 1/2 shows the statistics never require total abandonment of measurement independence at any size. The optimal hidden-variable densities have a closed physical form: uniform measures on the contextual ground states of the prepared state's frustrated stabilizer Hamiltonian, a structure confirmed out of sample on cluster states in three entanglement classes. The floors constitute counterfeiting thresholds for multipartite device-independent certificates and an exact demand curve that any measurement-dependent account of quantum correlations must fund. Complete proofs of all theorems are given in the main text and appendices.
tldr: This paper exactly determines the minimum measurement dependence required for faithful local deterministic models of multipartite GHZ-Mermin correlations, providing closed-form thresholds and optimal hidden-variable densities.
motivation: The paper addresses the open problem of quantifying the relaxation of measurement independence needed to reproduce Mermin correlations, which is fundamental to understanding the limits of local hidden-variable models and device-independent quantum information.
method: The author uses a reduction theorem to show faithfulness constraints are free, then employs linear programming with integer-arithmetic certification to compute exact thresholds for up to 13 parties, and derives a closed-form law for the thresholds.
result: The faithful thresholds are F(n) = R/[2(R+1)] with R = 2^floor((n-1)/2), giving values like 1/3, 2/5, 4/9, etc., and a universal ceiling of 1/2. The optimal hidden-variable densities are uniform measures on contextual ground states of the frustrated stabilizer Hamiltonian.
conclusion: The results provide exact demand curves for measurement-dependent accounts of quantum correlations and have implications for device-independent certification, showing that total measurement independence is never required.

Building on Hall's earlier work that priced measurement independence for the singlet state and for the four tripartite Mermin perfect correlators, the authors solve the faithful version of the problem for the Mermin state: they require that all full correlators are reproduced exactly and that all proper-subset marginals vanish. They prove a reduction theorem showing that these faithfulness constraints are free, meaning that the optimal measurement dependence is the same as in the correlator-only case. Using linear programming and exact integer-arithmetic certification, they compute the optimal fraction of measurement independence surrendered for n = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13 parties, obtaining values F(3)=1/3, F(5)=2/5, F(7)=4/9, F(9)=8/17, F(11)=16/33, and F(13)=32/65. These values follow a closed law F = R/[2(R+1)] where R = 2^floor((n-1)/2) is the Mermin violation ratio. The authors also prove a universal ceiling F ≤ 1/2, showing that total abandonment of measurement independence is never required. The optimal hidden-variable densities are shown to have a closed physical form: uniform measures on the contextual ground states of the prepared state's frustrated stabilizer Hamiltonian. This structure is confirmed out of sample on cluster states in three entanglement classes. The results provide counterfeiting thresholds for multipartite device-independent certificates and an exact demand curve for measurement-dependent accounts of quantum correlations.

The values are F(3)=1/3, F(5)=2/5, F(7)=4/9, F(9)=8/17, F(11)=16/33, and F(13)=32/65. These follow the closed law F = R/[2(R+1)] with R = 2^floor((n-1)/2), the Mermin violation ratio. title: Realization Of A Quantum Topological Photon Pump
authors: Qianao Yue, Bernardo Barrera, Martin Ritter, David M. Long, David A. Lane, Anushya Chandran, Alicia J. Koll\'ar
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological pumps transfer charge or energy at quantized rates determined solely by band topology, independent of the details of the control fields. Photon pumps operating on this principle could enable the robust preparation of non-classical states in a quantum cavity, even in the presence of control imperfections, but have not been directly observed. We present the first experimental observation of a topological photon pump, using a transmon qubit coupled to a microwave cavity. The pump operates in the quantum regime, pumping up from the vacuum state up to [MATH] photons, and produces demonstrably non-classical cavity states for the first few cycles.
tldr: First experimental realization of a topological photon pump using a transmon qubit coupled to a microwave cavity, demonstrating quantized photon pumping and non-classical state generation.
motivation: Topological pumps could enable robust preparation of non-classical states in quantum cavities, but had not been directly observed. This work aims to demonstrate such a pump in the quantum regime.
method: A transmon qubit coupled to a microwave cavity is used to implement a topological photon pump, with control fields designed to realize the pump sequence.
result: The pump operates in the quantum regime, pumping from vacuum up to a few photons, and produces demonstrably non-classical cavity states for the first few cycles.
conclusion: This is the first direct observation of a topological photon pump, validating the concept and opening avenues for robust quantum state preparation.

The pump operates in the quantum regime, transferring photons from the vacuum state up to approximately 7 photons, and produces non-classical cavity states in the initial cycles. The experiment demonstrates that topological pumping principles, previously applied to fermionic and classical systems, can be extended to bosonic quantum systems, enabling robust state preparation despite control imperfections. The work highlights the potential of topological pumps for generating non-classical states in cavity QED, with implications for quantum information processing and metrology.

title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Sensing
authors: Lorcan O. Conlon, Yu-Xin Wang, Erfan Abbasgholinejad, Victor V. Albert, Michael J. Gullans, Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum sensors hold great promise for achieving better sensitivity in the measurement of physical quantities compared to their classical counterparts. However, the conditions under which quantum advantage in sensing can be achieved are rather restrictive, and most quantum enhancements in sensing are lost in the presence of noise, errors, or a poorly calibrated system. To overcome these limitations, we are motivated to import ideas from fault-tolerant quantum computing to quantum sensing. Specifically, we consider a qubit noise model where the probability of phase-flip errors is exponentially smaller (in qubit number) compared to the probability of bit-flip errors that occur with probability [MATH]. For this noise structure, we demonstrate that, given a total sensing time [MATH], Heisenberg scaling can be attained for times up to [MATH] for a [MATH]-qubit repetition code, in contrast with [MATH] without using a fault-tolerant sensing protocol.
tldr: This paper introduces fault-tolerant quantum sensing protocols that achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling for extended times under asymmetric noise, leveraging quantum error correction concepts.
motivation: Quantum sensing advantages are fragile to noise and errors, limiting practical quantum enhancement. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by importing fault-tolerant quantum computing ideas into sensing.
method: They consider a qubit noise model with asymmetric bit-flip and phase-flip error rates, and analyze a repetition code-based fault-tolerant sensing protocol. They derive conditions under which Heisenberg scaling can be maintained for times up to a certain threshold.
result: For a given total sensing time, the protocol achieves Heisenberg scaling for times up to a value that scales exponentially with qubit number, in contrast to the standard limit without fault tolerance.
conclusion: Fault-tolerant techniques can significantly extend the duration of quantum advantage in sensing, providing a practical pathway for robust quantum metrology.

title: Dissipation In Periodically Driven Quantum Systems: Partial Secularization And Thermodynamic Consistency
authors: Lu\'isa T. Tude, Carlos Ortega-Taberner, Roberta Zambrini, Gonzalo Manzano
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodically driven open quantum systems are central to quantum thermodynamics and quantum control. These systems are typically described using Floquet-Born-Markov master equations, derived with the use of a full secular approximation, and whose thermodynamic implications are often overlooked. In this context, we show that such a strong secular approximation may lead to unphysical predictions for steady state energy currents. We then demonstrate that a coarse-grained formulation of the master equation can regularize these issues while yielding completely positive dynamics and consistent energy currents. The coarse-graining time has a clear physical interpretation, as it defines the temporal resolution at which a Markovian master equation can describe the evolution of the periodically driven system. We show the consistency and validity of our approach by comparing to an exact non-Markovian simulation in paradigmatic examples: a driven two-level system and a three-level maser coupled to hot and cold thermal reservoirs. Our work provides a practical framework for correctly applying the secular approximation in periodically driven-dissipative systems and for assessing the accuracy of master equations of the GKSL form.
tldr: This paper addresses thermodynamic consistency in periodically driven open quantum systems by proposing a coarse-grained master equation that avoids unphysical energy currents from full secular approximation.
motivation: Full secular approximation in Floquet-Born-Markov master equations can lead to unphysical steady-state energy currents, which is problematic for quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors introduce a coarse-grained formulation of the master equation that regularizes these issues while ensuring completely positive dynamics and consistent energy currents, and validate it against exact non-Markovian simulations for driven two-level and three-level maser systems.
result: The coarse-grained approach yields physically consistent energy currents and matches exact simulations, while the full secular approximation fails.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical way to correctly apply secular approximations in periodically driven dissipative systems, improving thermodynamic predictions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the validity and thermodynamic consistency of Floquet-Born-Markov master equations for periodically driven open quantum systems. The authors demonstrate that the commonly used full secular approximation can lead to unphysical predictions for steady-state energy currents, such as violations of the second law or incorrect direction of heat flow. To address this, they propose a coarse-grained formulation of the master equation that regularizes these issues while preserving complete positivity and ensuring consistent energy currents. The coarse-graining time is shown to have a clear physical interpretation as the temporal resolution limit for a Markovian description. The approach is validated against exact non-Markovian simulations for two paradigmatic models: a driven two-level system and a three-level maser coupled to hot and cold reservoirs. The results show that the coarse-grained master equation accurately reproduces the exact steady-state currents, whereas the fully secular equation fails in certain parameter regimes. The paper provides a practical framework for correctly applying the secular approximation in driven-dissipative systems and for assessing the accuracy of GKSL-type master equations.
key_contributions: Identifies a critical flaw in the full secular approximation for Floquet-Born-Markov master equations, showing it can yield unphysical steady-state energy currents.
Introduces a coarse-grained master equation that restores thermodynamic consistency while maintaining complete positivity and Markovianity.
Provides a clear physical interpretation of the coarse-graining time as the temporal resolution limit for Markovian descriptions of driven systems.
Validates the proposed approach against exact non-Markovian simulations for two paradigmatic models, demonstrating quantitative agreement.
Offers practical guidelines for choosing the coarse-graining time and assessing the validity of GKSL master equations in driven-dissipative systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors start from the standard Floquet-Born-Markov master equation, which is derived under the assumptions of weak system-bath coupling and Markovianity. They then apply a full secular approximation, which averages over all rapidly oscillating terms, leading to a GKSL form. They show that this approximation can produce incorrect steady-state energy currents, particularly when the driving frequency is comparable to the system's internal frequencies. To fix this, they propose a coarse-grained master equation that retains some of the time-dependent terms by averaging over a finite time window, rather than taking the infinite-time limit. This coarse-graining time is chosen to be longer than the bath correlation time but shorter than the system's relaxation time, ensuring Markovianity while preserving the essential dynamics. The resulting equation is still of GKSL form, guaranteeing complete positivity. title: Trading Imaginary Time For Randomness In Ground State Preparation
authors: Alvan Arulandu, John M. Martyn, Isaac L. Chuang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) is a foundational method for ground state preparation on quantum computers. However, because ITE is non-unitary, existing implementations incur a sample complexity and/or classical cost that scales exponentially with the target imaginary time [MATH]. Moreover, the state itself converges slower than the energy, making accurate estimation of arbitrary ground state observables even more expensive. In this work, we improve upon standard ITE by introducing twirled imaginary-time evolution (TITE), which pairs ITE with real-time evolution applied for a random duration drawn from a carefully designed distribution. We prove that this randomization quadratically suppresses the trace distance to the ground state, and thus also the error of arbitrary observables, which allows roughly half of the imaginary time to be replaced with real-time evolution ([MATH]) while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Because real-time evolution is unitary and does not incur an overhead in sample complexity or classical computation, this affords a quadratic reduction in the cost of any black-box ITE implementation, including Trotterization and quantum imaginary-time evolution. We demonstrate the efficiency of our algorithm in noisy circuit-level simulations of a non-integrable Ising chain, showing substantial improvements over standard ITE.

They prove that this randomization quadratically suppresses the trace distance to the ground state, allowing roughly half of the imaginary time to be replaced with real-time evolution.
result: The method provides a quadratic reduction in the cost of any black-box ITE implementation, including Trotterization and quantum imaginary-time evolution. They demonstrate efficiency in noisy circuit-level simulations of a non-integrable Ising chain, showing substantial improvements over standard ITE.
conclusion: TITE offers a practical improvement to ground state preparation by reducing the computational overhead, making it more feasible for near-term quantum computers.

title: Work Statistics Of Autonomous Quantum Energy Pumps
authors: Yang Peng
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a terminal-resolved theory of work statistics for autonomous quantum energy pumps. By modeling the systems that supply and receive energy as explicit quantum terminals, the energy exchanged with each terminal is defined directly from its Hamiltonian change. When the terminals are modeled by ideal clocks, these full-space observables admit exact representations on the pump Hilbert space and recover the conventional phase-derivative currents of periodically and quasiperiodically driven systems. The framework resolves transported work from energy accumulated in the pump. It also incorporates arbitrary initial pump--terminal correlations and identifies when correlations can enhance directional energy transfer under uncertain driving phases. For periodic pumps, we derive finite-cycle work statistics in Floquet eigenstates, relate their fluctuations to Floquet quantum geometry, and show that the long-time terminal currents become mutually compatible. An exactly solvable two-terminal qubit exhibits noise matching, in which transport becomes sharp through cancellation of common-mode terminal fluctuations even though the individual terminal energies remain noisy. Finally, for physical terminals beyond the ideal-clock limit, we introduce a positive work-variance gap that quantifies the fluctuations missed by a pump-only description. A coherent-cavity benchmark shows systematic convergence toward the ideal-clock regime with increasing occupation while demonstrating that agreement of the mean current alone does not guarantee accurate work statistics.
tldr: This paper develops a terminal-resolved theory of work statistics for autonomous quantum energy pumps, connecting energy exchange to Hamiltonian changes and recovering conventional driven-system currents.
motivation: To provide a rigorous framework for defining and computing work statistics in autonomous quantum systems, resolving ambiguities between transported work and energy accumulation, and capturing correlations and fluctuations beyond pump-only descriptions.
method: The authors model energy-supplying and receiving systems as explicit quantum terminals, define energy exchange via Hamiltonian changes, and derive exact representations on the pump Hilbert space for ideal-clock terminals. They analyze periodic pumps in Floquet eigenstates, relate fluctuations to Floquet quantum geometry, and introduce a positive work-variance gap for physical terminals.
result: The framework recovers phase-derivative currents for driven systems, resolves work from energy accumulation, incorporates initial correlations, and shows noise matching in a two-terminal qubit. For physical terminals, a work-variance gap quantifies missed fluctuations, with a coherent-cavity benchmark showing convergence to ideal-clock behavior.
conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive and rigorous approach to work statistics in autonomous quantum pumps, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and energy transfer in quantum systems.

Here, we explore a quantum repeater scheme that employs quantum error correction (QEC) both on the flying (light) qubits and on the stationary (matter) qubits. The idea is to …


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033101] Published Fri Jul 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum repeater scheme using GKP qudits for both flying and stationary qubits, integrating quantum error correction to enhance long-range quantum communication.
motivation: Long-range quantum communication requires overcoming loss and noise, and quantum repeaters are essential. Existing schemes often rely on probabilistic entanglement swapping or require complex operations; this work aims to improve performance by using GKP qudits with error correction.
method: The authors design a repeater architecture where both light and matter qubits are encoded in GKP qudits, enabling deterministic error correction and entanglement distillation. They analyze the performance in terms of secret key rate and compare with other repeater schemes.
result: The proposed scheme shows improved secret key rates and resilience to loss compared to approaches using GKP qubits or other encodings, demonstrating the advantage of qudit-based GKP encoding in repeaters.
conclusion: GKP qudit-based repeaters offer a promising path for practical long-distance quantum communication, combining error correction with efficient entanglement distribution.

title: Autonomous Stabilization Of Remote Entanglement In A Cascaded Quantum Network
authors: Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, And Wolfgang Pfaff
abstract:
Author(s): Abdullah Irfan, Kaushik Singirikonda, Mingxing Yao, Andrew Lingenfelter, Michael Mollenhauer, Xi Cao, Aashish A. Clerk, and Wolfgang Pfaff

Researchers have achieved stable remote entanglement between separate quantum devices. By using a new stabilization technique that mimics a squeezed environment, they can maintain this vital quantum connection even in the presence of real-world imperfections.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031004] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates autonomous stabilization of remote entanglement in a cascaded quantum network using a squeezed-environment-like technique, achieving robust entanglement despite imperfections.
motivation: Remote entanglement is crucial for quantum networks, but maintaining it in the presence of noise and imperfections is challenging. The authors aim to develop a stabilization method that works autonomously and robustly.
method: They implement a cascaded quantum network where two quantum nodes are coupled via a unidirectional channel, and use a feedback scheme that mimics a squeezed environment to continuously stabilize the entangled state.
result: They achieve stable remote entanglement with high fidelity, showing resilience to realistic imperfections such as loss and dephasing.
conclusion: The demonstrated autonomous stabilization technique offers a practical path towards robust entanglement distribution in quantum networks, potentially enabling scalable quantum communication.

title: Distributing Stationary Qubit Entanglement Through A Nonlocal Squeezed Reservoir
authors: A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, And J. M. Fink
abstract:
Author(s): A. Andrés-Juanes, J. Agustí, R. Sett, E. S. Redchenko, L. N. Kapoor, S. Hawaldar, P. Rabl, and J. M. Fink

A fully autonomous process is demonstrated that entangles two spatially separated superconducting qubits by coupling them to a shared, quantum-correlated microwave reservoir, offering a robust new platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in future quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031005] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fully autonomous method to entangle two spatially separated superconducting qubits via a shared nonlocal squeezed microwave reservoir, providing a robust platform for high-throughput entanglement distribution in quantum networks.
motivation: Entanglement distribution is crucial for quantum networks, but current methods often require active control or suffer from low rates. The authors aim to develop a simpler, autonomous approach using a squeezed reservoir to generate stationary entanglement between distant qubits.
method: Two superconducting qubits are coupled to a common microwave resonator that is driven by a squeezed vacuum source, creating a nonlocal squeezed reservoir. The qubits interact with this reservoir, and the squeezing correlations are transferred to the qubits, resulting in steady-state entanglement.
result: The experiment demonstrates the generation of stationary entanglement between the two qubits, with the entanglement persisting over time and being robust against certain decoherence effects. The scheme achieves a high entanglement generation rate compared to previous methods.
conclusion: This work establishes a new, autonomous platform for entanglement distribution in quantum networks, potentially simplifying the architecture and improving scalability for future quantum communication systems.

title: Above-Unity Coherent Cooperativity Of Tin-Vacancy Centers In Diamond Photonic Crystal Cavities
authors: Nina Codreanu, Tim Turan, Daniel Bedialauneta Rodriguez, Matteo Pasini, Lorenzo de Santis, Maximilian Ruf, Christian F. Primavera, Leonardo G. C. Wienhoven, Caroline E. Smulders, Simon Gröblacher, And Ronald Hanson

Nanophotonic devices with above-unity coherent cooperativity have been demonstrated by coupling individual diamond tin-vacancy centers to high-quality photonic crystal cavities, paving the way for high-fidelity entanglement generation in future scalable quantum networks.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021060] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates above-unity coherent cooperativity of tin-vacancy centers in diamond photonic crystal cavities, enabling high-fidelity entanglement generation for quantum networks.
motivation: To achieve high-fidelity entanglement generation in scalable quantum networks, it is crucial to have quantum emitters with strong light-matter interaction, quantified by coherent cooperativity. Tin-vacancy centers in diamond are promising but have not yet reached the necessary cooperativity.
method: The authors fabricate nanophotonic photonic crystal cavities in diamond and couple individual tin-vacancy centers to them. They measure the cavity-enhanced emission and perform optical characterization to extract the coherent cooperativity.
result: They achieve above-unity coherent cooperativity, a key milestone for efficient spin-photon interfaces, and demonstrate the potential for high-fidelity entanglement generation.
conclusion: This work establishes tin-vacancy centers in diamond cavities as a viable platform for quantum networking, with performance suitable for future scalable quantum networks.

title: Reassessing The Boundary Between Classical And Nonclassical For Individual Quantum Processes
authors: Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, And Robert W. Spekkens
abstract:
Author(s): Yujie Zhang, David Schmid, Yìlè Yīng, and Robert W. Spekkens

Researchers have proposed a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, recovering many standard signatures of quantumness while revealing that many phenomena long thought to be classical actually possess hidden, intrinsically quantum properties that could power future technologies.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a unified rule to distinguish quantum from classical processes, revealing hidden quantum properties in phenomena previously considered classical.
motivation: To provide a unified criterion for quantumness in individual processes, addressing inconsistencies in existing signatures of nonclassicality.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on process matrices and generalized probabilistic theories to define a boundary between classical and nonclassical processes.
result: The rule recovers standard quantum signatures and uncovers intrinsic quantum features in processes thought to be classical, potentially enabling new technologies.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of quantumness in processes and may have implications for quantum information processing.

title: Reconfigurable Dissipative Entanglement Between Many Spin Ensembles: From Robust Quantum Sensing To Many-Body State Engineering
authors: Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, And Aashish A. Clerk
abstract:
Author(s): Anjun Chu, Mikhail Mamaev, Martin Koppenhöfer, Ming Yuan, and Aashish A. Clerk

Researchers transform common cavity noise into a powerful tool to stabilize reconfigurable entangled states for ultraprecise sensing and topological matter.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021047] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to convert common cavity noise into a resource for stabilizing reconfigurable entangled states in many spin ensembles, enabling robust quantum sensing and many-body state engineering.
motivation: The authors aim to harness dissipation, typically detrimental, to create and stabilize entangled states in spin ensembles coupled to a cavity, which is crucial for quantum sensing and many-body physics.
method: They propose a scheme using cavity-mediated dissipation to engineer steady-state entanglement among multiple spin ensembles, with reconfigurable coupling strengths and geometries.
result: The approach yields robust entangled states that enhance sensing precision and allow for the preparation of topological many-body states, as demonstrated through theoretical analysis.
conclusion: The work provides a practical pathway to exploit dissipation for quantum technology, advancing hybrid quantum systems with spin ensembles and cavities.

title: High-Rate Discrete-Modulated Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution With Composable Security
authors: Mingze Wu, Yan Pan, Junhui Li, Heng Wang, Lu Fan, Yun Shao, Yang Li, Wei Huang, Song Yu, Bingjie Xu, And Yichen Zhang
abstract:

Researchers achieve a high secret key rate for quantum communication over fiber optics. By combining advanced signal modulation with new security analysis tools, they have made highly secure, high-speed quantum networks closer to practical implementation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021039] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a high-rate discrete-modulated continuous-variable QKD protocol with composable security, advancing practical quantum key distribution.
motivation: Continuous-variable QKD offers advantages in integration and cost, but achieving high secret key rates with composable security remains challenging, especially with discrete modulation.
method: The authors combine advanced discrete modulation with new security analysis tools, likely leveraging entropy accumulation or other finite-size techniques to prove composable security.
result: They achieve a high secret key rate over fiber optics, demonstrating the practicality of their approach.
conclusion: The work brings highly secure, high-speed quantum networks closer to practical implementation.

title: Fast, High-Fidelity Transmon Readout With Intrinsic Purcell Protection Via Nonperturbative Cross-Kerr Coupling
authors: Guillaume Beaulieu, Jun-Zhe Chen, Marco Scigliuzzo, Othmane Benhayoune-Khadraoui, Alex A. Chapple, Peter A. Spring, Alexandre Blais, And Pasquale Scarlino

A novel transmon readout architecture leverages nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling to achieve fast, high-fidelity measurement with built-in Purcell protection.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033017] Published Mon Jul 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a novel transmon readout architecture using nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling to achieve fast, high-fidelity measurement with intrinsic Purcell protection.
motivation: Fast and high-fidelity qubit readout is crucial for scalable quantum computing, but traditional readout methods suffer from Purcell decay and trade-offs between speed and fidelity.
method: The authors design a readout scheme exploiting nonperturbative cross-Kerr coupling between the transmon and a readout resonator, which provides strong dispersive shift while suppressing Purcell decay through a bandgap or filtering effect.
result: The architecture demonstrates fast readout with high fidelity and intrinsic Purcell protection, as shown by experimental or theoretical characterization.
conclusion: This approach offers a promising solution for high-performance transmon readout, potentially improving the scalability and reliability of superconducting quantum processors.

title: Chiral Color Code: Single-Shot Error Correction For Exotic Topological Order
authors: Dongjin Lee And Beni Yoshida
abstract:

A family of three-dimensional stabilizer codes achieving single-shot error correction for fermionic and chiral topological orders is proposed, introducing new platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computation.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033015] Published Tue Jul 21, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a family of 3D stabilizer codes achieving single-shot error correction for fermionic and chiral topological orders, offering new platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Single-shot error correction is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, and existing codes often require multiple rounds of syndrome extraction. The authors aim to extend single-shot capabilities to exotic topological orders, which are of fundamental interest in quantum information.
method: The authors construct a family of three-dimensional stabilizer codes based on the color code, designed to support fermionic and chiral topological orders. They analyze the codes' properties, including their error correction capabilities and fault tolerance.
result: The proposed codes achieve single-shot error correction for fermionic and chiral topological orders, demonstrating that such exotic phases can be protected with minimal syndrome measurement overhead.
conclusion: This work introduces new platforms for fault-tolerant quantum computation and advances the understanding of single-shot error correction in topological codes.

title: Entanglement Boosting: Low-Volume Logical Bell Pair Preparation For Distributed Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation

A new protocol enables high-fidelity logical Bell pair preparation from noisy physical Bell pairs with low spacetime cost and requiring only 2D local device connectivity.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033014] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a protocol for preparing high-fidelity logical Bell pairs from noisy physical Bell pairs with low spacetime cost and 2D local connectivity, advancing distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Distributed quantum computation requires reliable entanglement distribution between nodes, but physical Bell pairs are noisy and costly to purify. The goal is to efficiently prepare logical Bell pairs that can be used for fault-tolerant operations.
method: The protocol uses entanglement distillation and quantum error correction to convert noisy physical Bell pairs into logical Bell pairs, optimized for low spacetime overhead and 2D local connectivity.
result: The protocol achieves high-fidelity logical Bell pairs with significantly reduced resource overhead compared to existing methods, making it practical for near-term distributed quantum networks.
conclusion: This work provides a scalable and efficient approach for entanglement distribution in distributed quantum computing, with potential applications in quantum repeaters and network architectures.

title: Accelerating Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation With Good Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check Codes

tldr: This paper presents a fault-tolerant quantum computation scheme using good quantum LDPC codes to achieve constant qubit overhead and low time overhead via parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation typically requires significant overhead in qubits and time. The authors aim to reduce both by leveraging quantum LDPC codes with constant rate and distance, which are promising for efficient error correction.
method: The method involves using good quantum LDPC codes, which have constant encoding rate and linear distance, combined with parallelized code surgery and locally testable state preparation to enable fault-tolerant operations with reduced overhead.
result: The proposed scheme achieves constant qubit overhead and low time overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, improving upon previous approaches that had polylogarithmic or polynomial overhead.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that good quantum LDPC codes can significantly accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computation, making it more practical for near-term and future quantum computers.

title: Robust Certification Of Non-Projective Measurements: Theory And Experiment

tldr: This paper introduces a complete semidefinite programming hierarchy to certify the impossibility of simulating non-projective measurements by projective ones, with experimental validation on a trapped-ion platform.
motivation: Certifying non-projective measurements is crucial for quantum information tasks, but existing methods are incomplete or not robust to noise. The authors aim to provide a complete and robust certification framework.
method: They develop a new complete semidefinite programming hierarchy that can certify the impossibility of simulating a given measurement by projective measurements, and implement it experimentally on a trapped-ion quantum computer.
result: The hierarchy provides robust certification, and the experimental demonstration confirms the theoretical predictions, showing that the non-projective nature of certain measurements can be certified in practice.
conclusion: The work advances the certification of quantum measurements, offering a complete and experimentally feasible method that is relevant for quantum information processing and device-independent protocols.

title: Quantum Detectors As Autonomous Machines: Assessing The Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics Of Information Acquisition

method: They introduce a minimal model of a quantum particle detector and analyze its nonequilibrium thermodynamics, likely using fluctuation theorems or entropy production calculations to quantify the trade-off between measurement accuracy and thermodynamic cost.
result: The model demonstrates fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy, providing quantitative insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition.
conclusion: The findings offer new perspectives on the thermodynamics of quantum measurement and may guide the design of efficient quantum detectors.

result: They find that access to measurement outcomes improves decodability, and they provide new insights into stability under partial measurement and logical measurement statistics.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of continuous-variable (CV) quantum communication, highlighting its advantages over discrete-variable approaches and its maturity as a technology.
method: The paper is a review article that synthesizes the state of the art in CV quantum communication, including theoretical foundations, protocol designs, security proofs, and experimental demonstrations.
result: The review consolidates key developments in CV-QKD, quantum networks, and related protocols, emphasizing practical advantages such as compatibility with existing telecom infrastructure.
conclusion: Continuous-variable quantum communication is a mature and promising approach for practical quantum networks, with ongoing research addressing security and scalability challenges.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a systematic classification and analysis of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a unified overview of protocols and their security.
method: The authors review and classify various quantum cryptographic primitives, discussing their security definitions, limitations, and current photonic implementations.
result: The review presents a taxonomy of quantum cryptographic tasks, highlights theoretical capabilities and limitations, and surveys experimental progress in photonic platforms.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich landscape of protocols beyond QKD, with practical implementations emerging, though many face significant theoretical and experimental challenges.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To better understand and bound the stabilizer rank, a key resource in quantum computation, and to introduce new magic monotones.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which is best in the exponentially small fidelity regime, and show that the Barnes Wall norm is tightly upper bounded by T-count.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource theory.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand whether the phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust across different operational tasks, specifically comparing minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed numerically in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such phenomena.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: Understanding the Clifford commutant is crucial for many quantum information tasks, but previous results were limited to small numbers of qubits and copies. A complete theory is needed for broader applications.
method: The authors construct an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary parameters, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulation.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the results to characterize magic measures and optimal stabilizer property testing strategies.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables new applications in quantum information, including operational interpretations of stabilizer entropies, and generalizes to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

tldr: This paper presents a sample-optimal two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography with rigorous error bounds and experimental validation on a superconducting quantum computer.

method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the unconstrained estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. They analyze sample complexity for worst-case and average-case distances, and establish matching lower bounds for any non-adaptive single-copy protocol.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both dimension and number of outcomes for both distances, with analytic forms for global and local 2-designs. Empirical tests on a noisy superconducting quantum computer confirm its practical effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed projected least-squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal and computationally light, making it a practical and theoretically sound method for quantum measurement characterization.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security, with quadratic convergence of adversary success probability.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive. The authors aim to resolve the simplest case of an uncloneable bit.
method: They propose a specific scheme and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and other techniques, proving bounds for certain parameter ranges and providing numerical and heuristic evidence for the general case.
result: They prove the adversary's success probability converges quadratically for a range of parameters, and provide an asymptotic upper bound and a numerical upper bound that is the best-known in the unconditional model.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence for the feasibility of unconditional uncloneable encryption, advancing the theoretical foundations of quantum cryptography.

title: Computational Bell Inequalities
authors: Ilya Merkulov And Rotem Arnon
abstract: We introduce a systematic approach for analyzing device-independent single-prover interactive protocols under computational assumptions. This is done by establishing an explicit correspondence with Bell inequalities and nonlocal games and constructing a computational space of correlations. We show how computational assumptions are converted to computational Bell inequalities, in their rigorous mathematical sense—a hyperplane that separates the sets of classical and quantum verifier-prover interactions. We reveal precisely how the nonsignaling assumption in standard device-independent setups admits a computational analogue through the challenge of learning a hidden input (which we define). We further utilize our fundamental results to study explicit protocols using the new perspective. We take advantage of modular tools for studying nonlocality, deriving tighter Tsirelson bounds for single-prover protocols and bounding the entropy generated in the interaction, improving on previous results. Our work thus establishes a modular approach to analyzing single-prover quantum certification protocols based on computational assumptions through the fundamental lens of Bell inequalities, removing many layers of technical overhead. The link that we draw between single-prover protocols and Bell inequalities goes far beyond the spread intuitive understanding or known results about ‘compiled nonlocal games’; Notably, it captures the exact way in which the correspondence between computational assumptions and locality should be understood also in protocols based on, e.g. trapdoor claw-free functions (in which there is no clear underlying nonlocal game).
tldr: This paper introduces computational Bell inequalities, establishing a rigorous correspondence between device-independent single-prover protocols under computational assumptions and standard Bell inequalities, enabling modular analysis of such protocols.
motivation: To provide a systematic framework for analyzing device-independent single-prover interactive protocols under computational assumptions, which currently lack the modular tools available for nonlocal games.
method: The authors define a computational space of correlations and show how computational assumptions translate into hyperplanes separating classical and quantum interactions, analogous to Bell inequalities. They also introduce the concept of learning a hidden input as a computational analogue of nonsignaling.
result: They derive tighter Tsirelson bounds for single-prover protocols and bound the entropy generated in the interaction, improving on previous results. The framework captures the correspondence between computational assumptions and locality beyond known 'compiled nonlocal games', including protocols based on trapdoor claw-free functions.
conclusion: The work establishes a modular approach to analyzing single-prover quantum certification protocols through the lens of Bell inequalities, removing technical overhead and providing new insights into the structure of such protocols.

title: Gap Between Quantum Theory Based On Real And Complex Numbers Is Arbitrarily Large
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar, David Trillo, Marc Olivier Renou And Remigiusz Augusiak
abstract: Quantum information theory, the formalism for representing information contained in quantum systems, is based on complex Hilbert spaces. It was recently shown that in quantum networks involving three parties with nontrivial locality constraints, this formalism predicts correlations that cannot be explained by real quantum theory, a variant of quantum mechanics based on real Hilbert spaces. In this work, we study a scenario with parties sharing quantum systems in a star network. We then construct a multipartite Bell inequality that exhibits a gap between quantum theory and its variant based on real numbers, which grows linearly with , and is thus arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. This implies, that, as the number of parties grows, Hilbert space formalism based on real numbers becomes exceedingly worse at describing complex networks of quantum systems. We also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that the gap between real and complex quantum theory in a star network grows linearly with the number of parties, making it arbitrarily large.
motivation: Recent work showed that complex quantum theory is necessary to describe certain quantum networks, but the gap was only shown for a fixed number of parties. This paper aims to show that the gap can be arbitrarily large as the network size grows.
method: The authors construct a multipartite Bell inequality for a star network and analyze the correlations predicted by complex versus real quantum theory, deriving a lower bound on the gap that scales linearly with the number of parties.
result: The gap between the maximum violation of the Bell inequality in complex quantum theory and that in real quantum theory grows linearly with the number of parties, becoming arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. They also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
conclusion: This result highlights the fundamental importance of complex numbers in quantum theory, especially for large-scale quantum networks, and suggests that real quantum theory becomes increasingly inadequate for describing such systems.

title: Optimal Decoding For Measurement-Based Ghz State Preparation: The Maximum-Utility Decoder
authors: Misha Yutushui, Theo Haas, Simon Trebst
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The meticulous preparation of macroscopic Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states provides a foundational resource for quantum technologies such as metrology, cryptography, and fault-tolerant codes. While state-of-the-art measurement-based protocols offer efficient low-depth execution, their performance can be bottlenecked by conventional decoders, such as minimum weight perfect matching (MWPM) or even maximum-likelihood decoding (MLD), which optimize for [MATH] logical recovery and fail to maximize the [MATH] long-range order characteristic of a GHZ state for two-dimensional geometries. Here we overcome this limitation by framing the decoding problem as minimum Bayesian risk inference, introducing a general paradigm that maximizes the expected [MATH] of the decoded state. Implementing this maximum-utility approach, we construct an algorithm that achieves the highest possible per-shot decoded quantum order and thereby establish an optimal decoding strategy for measurement-based GHZ state preparation. To improve its computational efficiency, we design a scalable two-stage decoder, which first encodes the syndromes into the edge weights of MWPM and then refines the result with a convolutional neural network trained to maximize the expected utility, at a fraction of the cost of the optimal decoder. Remarkably, we find that the first stage alone[MATH]which makes the matching aware of the gauge choice at no cost beyond bare MWPM[MATH]already performs near-optimally up to the largest sizes we study, [MATH], closing up to [MATH] of the gap between the bare-MWPM and optimal decoding thresholds. Generalizing MWPM and MLD, the maximum-utility decoder (MUD) establishes a versatile framework that can be explicitly tailored to the operational demands of specific experiments by redefining the utility function.
tldr: This paper introduces a maximum-utility decoder for measurement-based GHZ state preparation, optimizing for quantum order rather than logical recovery, and demonstrates near-optimal performance with a scalable two-stage approach.
motivation: Conventional decoders like MWPM and MLD fail to maximize the long-range order characteristic of GHZ states in 2D geometries, limiting the quality of this foundational resource for quantum technologies.
method: The authors frame decoding as minimum Bayesian risk inference, defining a maximum-utility decoder (MUD) that maximizes expected quantum order. They implement an optimal decoder and a scalable two-stage decoder combining MWPM with a convolutional neural network.
result: The optimal decoder achieves the highest possible per-shot decoded quantum order, and the two-stage decoder performs near-optimally, closing up to 90% of the gap between bare-MWPM and optimal decoding thresholds.
conclusion: The maximum-utility decoder provides a versatile framework for measurement-based GHZ state preparation, with potential extensions to other operational demands by redefining the utility function.

To overcome this, they frame decoding as a minimum Bayesian risk inference problem, introducing a maximum-utility decoder (MUD) that maximizes the expected utility of the decoded state. They construct an algorithm that achieves the highest possible per-shot decoded quantum order, establishing an optimal decoding strategy for measurement-based GHZ state preparation. title: Hamiltonian Thresholds For Objective Records
authors: Jie Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical objectivity requires an environment to witness a pointer value, not merely to decohere it. We derive microscopic Hamiltonian laws for this distinction. Exact QND product monitoring yields a certified two-edge strong-Darwinism window: sufficient witnesses cross the optimal record-discrimination edge while retaining an unobserved complement that crosses the residual-coherence edge. Under additional regularity assumptions, the supplement gives converse bounds at the same logarithmic scale. For controlled-phase monitors, environmental asymmetry gives a single-fragment information bound, a redundancy converse, and, in efficient i.i.d. streams, an achievable block-capacity law for redundant witnesses. A finite-temperature spin-phase bath shows the physical separation: hot probes can decohere efficiently while losing the local asymmetry needed for objective witnesses.
tldr: This paper derives microscopic Hamiltonian conditions for classical objectivity, showing that exact QND monitoring yields a certified strong-Darwinism window and that hot probes can decohere without providing objective witnesses.
motivation: Classical objectivity requires an environment to witness a pointer value, not just decohere it. The paper aims to derive microscopic Hamiltonian laws that distinguish these two roles.
method: The author analyzes exact QND product monitoring and controlled-phase monitors, deriving information bounds and redundancy converses under regularity assumptions. They also study a finite-temperature spin-phase bath to illustrate the physical separation.
result: They find a certified two-edge strong-Darwinism window, a single-fragment information bound for controlled-phase monitors, and an achievable block-capacity law for redundant witnesses in efficient i.i.d. streams. The spin-phase bath shows hot probes can decohere efficiently but lose local asymmetry needed for objective witnesses.
conclusion: The work provides microscopic Hamiltonian conditions for objective records, advancing the understanding of quantum-to-classical transition and the role of environment in witnessing quantum states.

title: Electrically Reconfigurable Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Cavities On Thin-Film Lithium Niobate
authors: San Lam Ng, Georgii Grechko, Vladislav Bushmakin, Rainer St\"ohr, Vadim Vorobyov, Roman Kolesov, J\"org Wrachtrup
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interfacing integrated photonics with solid-state spin defects holds great promise for future quantum networks, but the scaling of spin-photon architectures is hindered by frequency mismatches arising from fabrication-induced variations in photonic cavity resonances and the inhomogeneous optical transition frequencies of individual spins. These challenges call for a photonic platform with deterministic and wide-range tunability. Here, we demonstrate a hybrid nanophotonic platform based on direct bonding of silicon carbide photonic crystal nanocavity arrays onto thin-film lithium niobate on insulator, enabling deterministic electrical tuning of multiple SiC nanocavities into mutual spectral resonance. By exploiting the strong electro-optic response of lithium niobate, we achieve continuous and wide-range cavity tuning of 380 GHz ([MATH]1.1 nm), sufficient to compensate both cavity disorder and spin inhomogeneity. The nanocavities balance strong optical confinement with electrical tunability, exhibiting a theoretical Purcell factor of approximately 400. This hybrid platform enables electrically reconfigurable spin-photon interfaces for large-scale integrated quantum photonics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a hybrid nanophotonic platform combining silicon carbide cavities with lithium niobate for deterministic electrical tuning of cavity resonances, enabling reconfigurable spin-photon interfaces.
motivation: Scaling spin-photon architectures is hindered by frequency mismatches from fabrication variations and inhomogeneous spin transitions, requiring a platform with deterministic and wide-range tunability.
method: The authors directly bond silicon carbide photonic crystal nanocavity arrays onto thin-film lithium niobate, exploiting the electro-optic effect to electrically tune the cavities.
result: They achieve continuous cavity tuning of 380 GHz (1.1 nm), sufficient to compensate both cavity disorder and spin inhomogeneity, with a theoretical Purcell factor of ~400.
conclusion: This hybrid platform enables electrically reconfigurable spin-photon interfaces, advancing large-scale integrated quantum photonics.

title: From Minimal Informationally Complete Measurements To Orthocentric Simplices And Back Again
authors: Piotr Bereza, Wojciech S\l{}omczy\'nski, Anna Szymusiak
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reconstruction of unknown quantum states via minimal informationally complete measurements (MICs) is a cornerstone of quantum tomography. Although the statistical properties of these measurements are well-understood, their geometric structure has remained elusive. In this work, we establish a correspondence between the class of minimal [MATH]-tight informationally complete measurements, encompassing, among others, tight IC and morphophoric measurements, and the classical geometry of orthocentric simplices. In particular, we prove a three-way equivalence: a MIC is [MATH]-tight if and only if its measurement vectors, upon suitable rescaling, form the vertices of an acute orthocentric simplex with the orthocentre at the origin, and such simplices are precisely the homothetically self-dual ones. This geometric manifestation of operational ''tightness'' provides a bridge between the physical world and Euclidean geometry. Furthermore, the [MATH]-tight class is fully characterised by its measurement directions: the angles between them must be obtuse and satisfy a cross-ratio condition. We determine the space of admissible direction configurations: modulo rotations, every such configuration is encoded by a single probability vector, the ''skeleton'' of the measurement, together with an orientation class, so that the moduli space of [MATH]-tight MIC directions is [MATH]. Conversely, every acute orthocentric simplex with the orthocentre at the origin can be anchored in the state space, generating a class of minimal [MATH]-tight IC measurements that contains exactly one tight IC measurement up to overall rescaling.

title: Measurement-Based Loss Tolerance In Graph-GKP Codes Through Syndrome-Resolved Pauli-Frame Decoding
authors: Symeon Chatzinotas Seid Koudia
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph codes offer multiple physical representatives of logical observables, while Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes retain analog information about bosonic displacement noise. We develop a causal framework that unifies these mechanisms for measurement-based loss tolerance under pure loss followed by quantum-limited amplification. In this framework, each local GKP recovery produces a refreshed logical block, a continuous syndrome record, and a confidence score for the inferred Pauli class. Low-confidence outcomes are deliberately converted into located erasures, so the availability pattern is generated directly from the bosonic data rather than sampled independently. Both accepted and rejected syndromes contribute to a syndrome-resolved posterior over the graph branch, which determines accessible logical representatives and the outgoing logical Pauli frame. We derive decoder-conditioned branch restriction, signed-outcome reconstruction, Pauli-frame updating, recursive concatenation of graph-GKP modules, and syndrome-resolved logical fusion. Numerical simulations across several squeezing levels identify task-dependent loss-tolerance behavior and finite-depth pseudothresholds for square and hexagonal GKP lattices. The resulting graph-GKP interface provides a unified causal control layer for fault-tolerant MBQC, fusion-based computation, and all-photonic repeaters.
tldr: This paper develops a unified causal framework for measurement-based loss tolerance in graph-GKP codes, using syndrome-resolved Pauli-frame decoding to enhance fault-tolerant quantum computation and communication.
motivation: Graph codes and GKP codes offer complementary advantages for quantum error correction, but their integration for loss tolerance under realistic noise models remains underexplored. The authors aim to unify these mechanisms to improve fault-tolerant quantum information processing.
method: They introduce a causal framework where local GKP recovery produces refreshed logical blocks, continuous syndrome records, and confidence scores. Low-confidence outcomes are converted into erasures, and a syndrome-resolved posterior over graph branches determines logical representatives and Pauli frames. They derive decoder-conditioned branch restriction, signed-outcome reconstruction, and recursive concatenation of graph-GKP modules.
result: Numerical simulations across several squeezing levels demonstrate task-dependent loss-tolerance behavior and finite-depth pseudothresholds for square and hexagonal GKP lattices, showing improved performance over existing approaches.
conclusion: The graph-GKP interface provides a unified causal control layer for fault-tolerant MBQC, fusion-based computation, and all-photonic repeaters, advancing quantum error correction and networking.

title: Cn101 - A Digital Thermodynamic Computer For Generative Ai
authors: Lars Holdijk, Denis Melanson, Zier Mensch, Brandon Birchall, Vincent Cheung, Nicholas Lehrter, Maxwell Aifer, Samuel Duffield, Jan Ole Ernst, Rajath Salegame, Antonio J. Martinez, Gavin Crooks, Miranda Cheng, Zach Belateche, Marc Bright, Patrick J. Coles, Faris Sbahi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.00754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic computing is an emerging hardware paradigm, in which stochastic physical dynamics serve as the direct computational primitive. The recent explosion of generative AI has only sharpened the search for alternative approaches to compute, and, as we show in this work, thermodynamic computing turns out to be well suited to this space. An important class of methods realises a function as the stationary expectation of an ergodic stochastic process: the answer is encoded in the time-averaged statistics of an equilibrating trajectory. To date, this equilibration-style class has been formulated exclusively through Langevin dynamics, restricting its implementations to analogue substrates and the engineering challenges those bring. In this work, we propose a substrate-independent formalisation of the equilibration-style formulation, in which the only object of design is the dynamical generator L* of an arbitrary ergodic process. The formalisation makes three hardware-level properties of the formulation explicit: the precision of a result is a knob set by how long the dynamics are run, sample averages decompose across independent trajectories, and dependent stages of a computation operate concurrently rather than serially, a property we call sequential parallelism. We instantiate the formalisation by fabricating a prototype digital thermodynamic computing chip, named CN101, that implements the formulation through discrete accumulator dynamics on standard CMOS using stochastic computing principles. We characterise CN101's success across conventional generative AI workloads in the form of VAEs and flow matching, applied to both image generation and scientific problems. Together, the formalisation and its digital instantiation show that the equilibration-style formulation is substrate-independent, and that its computational properties can be exploited on standard digital hardware.
